author: Gian López
abstract: The review process itself, held constant across every technology. This skill owns what gets reviewed, which standards apply to it, what earns the name finding, and how a finding is written — and deliberately owns no language rules, taking those instead from the best-practices skills already installed and from the repository's own conventions. It is built around one constraint: a review must be cheap enough to run on every change. The scope is taken from the argument rather than guessed, and the standards from the paths it touches; those standards load as a rule index plus the few rules the scope actually needs, never as a compiled document. It carries no defect taxonomy of its own — what counts as wrong is what a loaded rule says is wrong — and every candidate finding passes a three-part contract: an anchor in the scope, a rule as ground, and a minimal patch, or it is dropped. What remains is ranked by the impact its rule already declared, written as one block each, and closed with a single question about what to do next
